These unsightly brown

FIBROMYALGIA (stiff lamb disease, white muscle disease, adult onset

the base line

drink filtered —not distilled—water. Distilled water

avoid carbonated soft drinks which ALL are loaded with phosphates which

Reduce the amount of vitamin D intake to a maximum of 400 IU/day (this

Treatment of cerebrovascular disease

claims.claim_text: Yes — emphatically. claims.verbatim: Fat sources include whole milk, butter, ghee, apricot oil, and animal fats.

Eat two eggs

claims.claim_text: Yes, but only a trace — and it is not a reason to eat tuna. Germanium is a trace element Wallach prizes as an immune booster (it stimulates natural killer cells, interferon, macrophages and T-suppressor cells) and an oxygen-utilization cofactor, with deficiency typified by a severely reduced immune status, arthritis, osteoporosis, low energy and cancer. But tuna carries only about 2.3 ppm of germanium — actually less than ordinary beans at 4.67 ppm, and far below the germanium-rich healing herbs and foods like garlic, ginseng and shiitake mushrooms (100 to 2,000 ppm). So fish is a minor incidental source at best — not a meaningful way to get germanium.
claims.verbatim:
Food plants and animals contain small amounts of germanium (i.e. beans—
4.67 ppm, tuna—2.3 ppm).

claims.claim_text: Essential fatty acids are required every day at 3% of total daily calorie intake, or 9 g per day when supplemented in capsule form. The 9 g is one combined amount for the essential fatty acids together, not 9 g of each.
claims.verbatim:
Essential fatty acids are a
must and should be consumed at the rate of 3 percent of your total daily
calorie consumption or supplemented at the rate of 9 grams per day in
capsule form.

claims.claim_text: Wallach's origin story for plant-derived colloidal minerals. He credits a specific product — Mineral Toddy, made by a company called Rockland U.S.A. — that he came across at Hospital Santa Monica. What made it work, he says, was where it came from: a prehistoric deposit of buried plant matter that had never turned into oil, coal, or stone. That escape from geological compression is why the minerals in it were still in the form the original plants had made them, ready for the body to use, rather than trapped back inside rock.
claims.verbatim:
Mineral Toddy was produced by Rockland U.S.A. from a unique prehistoric
plant deposit that had never been compressed into oil or coal. It had never
been fossilized or petrified.

claims.claim_text: Two claims about the same liquid, side by side. First: it carries 77 different minerals — more than the 60 Wallach counts as essential to a human body, so a single bottle covers the full essential spectrum and then some. Second: up to 98% of what you swallow is 'bio-available,' meaning the body can actually absorb and use it rather than pass it straight through. Both, in his framing, follow from the same fact: these minerals were built by living plants, not milled out of rock. A mineral's usefulness, to him, depends on which of those two things made it.
claims.verbatim:
The value of this tea colored liquid was that it
contained 77 minerals in the plant derived colloidal form. Because they
were plant derived colloidal minerals instead of from ground up rocks, they
were up to 98 percent bio-available.

claims.claim_text: The single step at the heart of Wallach's whole mineral framework — and the reason he cares about the source. Rock ground into fine dust and suspended in water is real minerals, but in a form that living cells can't take in. Plants can. Their roots pull those rock minerals up from the soil and rebuild them inside their own cells into a different chemical form — the form every living cell of every plant, animal, and human is actually built out of. So a mineral in a rock and the same mineral in a piece of broccoli, he argues, are not the same nutrient. A plant is the factory that does the one step your body can't do for itself, which is why he says the source matters.
claims.verbatim:
Plants, including wild forms and crops such as grains, vegetables, fruits,
and nuts, take up these inorganic metallic colloids and convert them into
intracellular (within the cell) organically bound plant colloids. These
organic plant colloids are the form of minerals found in and used by all
living cells of plants, animals, and humans.

claims.claim_text: 'Age Beaters' is Wallach's shorthand for the eight unrelated long-lived cultures he tracks — populations where reaching 100+ in good health is common rather than exceptional. What ties them together, he argues, is what grows in their fields: each settled by chance in a high arid valley below a glacier and built canals to bring the glacier's mineral-rich meltwater ('glacial milk') to their crops, which converted those inorganic minerals into plant-derived colloidal form. Those plant-derived colloidal minerals in their food, he says, are the common thread behind the shared longevity — and why he calls them, flatly, the Fountain of Youth.
claims.verbatim:
It is the plant derived colloidal minerals in their grains,
vegetables, fruits, and nuts that are their common threads giving the Age Beaters their health and longevity. It is the plant derived colloidal
minerals that are in fact the Fountain of Youth!

claims.claim_text: Wallach's own honest limit on Mineral Toddy, stated a few sentences after listing what it fixed. The colloidal liquid, he says, carries every mineral only in trace amounts. That is enough for the trace minerals the body needs in tiny amounts, but to even come close to the mainstream Recommended Daily Allowances it has to be paired with a separate source of what he calls the "major minerals and electrolytes": calcium, magnesium, manganese, zinc, and potassium. In the same passage he put the minerals in calcium-enriched orange juice, which both masked their harsh astringent taste and provided a significant amount of additional calcium — one of those lacking majors. On his own account the colloidal minerals were never meant as a stand-alone mineral supplement — a piece of the picture, not the whole picture.
claims.verbatim:
The colloidal
minerals were all present in trace amounts. They required an additional
source of the major minerals and electrolytes such as calcium, magnesium,
manganese, zinc, and potassium to even come close to the published RDAs.

claims.claim_text: Wallach's punchline to the entire search for longevity. For all of recorded history people have poured out resources, money, and even their lives chasing a Fountain of Youth — and his answer is almost anticlimactic: it was under our feet the whole time. The Fountain of Youth is minerals.
claims.verbatim:
The search for health and longevity is as old as man himself. We have
expended resources, money, energy, and have in fact died in droves looking
for the Fountain of Youth. Literally the Fountain of Youth has been under
our feet since the beginning of time. The answer is almost anticlimactic; it’s
minerals.

claims.claim_text: What the raw liquid actually tastes like. Plant-derived colloidal minerals are intensely astringent — Wallach says that taken straight, undiluted, they would 'shrink wrap your lips over your teeth.' That is why they are taken stirred into juice rather than drunk on their own.
claims.verbatim:
The plant derived colloidal minerals were very astringent. Taken “straight,”
they’d “shrink wrap your lips over your teeth” if you drank
them without juice.

claims.claim_text: How Wallach came to colloidal minerals. He had never even heard of them until he encountered the liquid being served to patients at Hospital Santa Monica. Excited by the new tool, he gathered every book and article ever written on colloids, and within three months had absorbed essentially everything then known about them.
claims.verbatim:
I got excited about this new-found nutritional tool, and I gathered every
piece of information that I could find on plant derived colloidal minerals. I
had never heard of colloidal minerals until this moment in my professional
career so I began to educate myself. I gathered every book and every article
that had ever been written on colloidal minerals and within three months I
was familiar with just about everything historically and currently known
about colloids and plant derived colloidal minerals.

claims.claim_text: Wallach's own account of the fight to keep plant-derived colloidal minerals high-quality — and a hard lesson about companies that cut corners. The minerals he built his products on came from one particular prehistoric deposit. When the company then bottling them, Eagle, quietly switched to a cheaper source to save about a dollar a gallon, the liquid changed batch to batch: one day thin and tasteless with its astringency gone, the next black like India ink, the next green. Every product built on those minerals suffered, and customers began complaining that 'the minerals didn't work anymore.' When Wallach objected, Eagle denied anything had changed, and in early 1997 terminated his distributorship, wanting a quieter corporate image. Rather than accept a degraded product, Wallach founded his own company, American Longevity, and went straight back to Elmer Heinrich of Rockland — the original deposit the minerals had come from since 1991 — relaunching them as 'Virgin Earth' plant-derived colloidal minerals. He went back to the proven source. The lasting lesson for anyone buying these minerals: the source deposit is what makes them work, and a cheaper source is not the same product.
claims.verbatim:
The Mineral Toddy, however, was beginning to change. One day you could
drink a quart of Toddy minerals like water because the astringent character
of the minerals was gone. The next batch of Mineral Toddy was black like
India Ink. The next batch was green. The obvious changes in the Mineral
Toddy negatively affected all of the products that used the minerals as a
base.

claims.claim_text: Wallach's opening thesis, framed as science. He treats the world's long-lived cultures as a living 'control group' — five ancient, very different peoples who all reached healthful, disease-free longevity, with steady access to all ninety essential nutrients the body needs. The secret they shared, he says, was unique natural sources of plant-derived colloidal minerals, and his promise is that anyone who taps that same accumulated knowledge can do the same.
claims.verbatim:
This control group of five
ancient and highly diverse cultures share common denominators that
include healthful, disease-free longevity, and unlimited access to adequate
levels of all ninety essential nutrients required by humans. One of the
secrets they shared includes access to unique natural sources of plant
derived colloidal minerals. My promise to you is that if you plug into the
thousands of years of accumulated knowledge of these long-lived peoples,
you and yours can make it too!

claims.claim_text: Microplastics are a modern problem Wallach's books never take up. But they fall squarely into a category he does address: xenobiotics — the foreign compounds the body has to recognize and clear. In a selenium review he quotes approvingly across several books, the mineral is described as 'involved in detoxification of metals and certain xenobiotics,' one of the body's built-in tools for handling foreign chemicals. From there his general defense against toxin load is consistent: keep selenium up (he runs 250 to 500 mcg a day in his prevention programs), lean on plant-derived colloidal minerals to 'reduce your risk of damage from heavy metals and pollution,' filter your home's water and air, and run a periodic detox. None of this is Wallach speaking about plastics specifically — it is his framework for foreign-chemical exposure, which microplastics now fall under.
claims.verbatim:
selenium acts as an acceptor of
biogenic methyl groups, and is involved in detoxification of metals and
certain xenobiotics. Selenium also has immunopotentiating properties.

claims.claim_text: As part of his cancer-prevention program, Wallach lays out a simple ongoing detox routine: take alfalfa daily 'in some form as a detoxifier,' do a liver flush once or twice a month by drinking apple juice for three days, and get a hair analysis each year — which he uses both to monitor toxic-metal load and to check how well you're absorbing minerals (if absorption is poor, he notes, all your mineral levels run low). It sits inside a broader daily regimen for keeping toxins down: dietary fiber at every meal, filtered (not distilled) water, 2 to 3 bowel movements a day, biodegradable household cleaners, and organic food wherever possible. The hair analysis is the feedback loop — it is how he would tell whether the metals are actually coming down.
claims.verbatim:
Take alfalfa daily in some form
as a detoxifier. Do a liver flush once or twice each month by drinking apple
juice for three days. Do a hair analysis each year to monitor toxic metal
load as well as absorption capability.

claims.claim_text: Achlorhydria — what causes it, and how common it is. Achlorhydria means the loss of the stomach's hydrochloric acid (HCl). Wallach names two causes, and says both run opposite to what most people assume. The first is stress — contrary to popular belief it does not raise stomach acid, it shuts acid production down, and he pins the moment: once stress passes the point of decompensation, where the body can no longer compensate. The second is age itself, a natural process he calls perhaps the most significant aging phenomenon, at 75 percent of people over 50 requiring supplemental stomach acid. A third contributor is dietary: ordinary salt (sodium chloride) is the raw material the stomach uses to manufacture its acid, so people on salt-restricted diets are more likely to become achlorhydric. The everyday sign is 'burp, belch, and bloat' after eating.
claims.verbatim:
ACHLORHYDRIA (loss of stomach acid—hydrochloric acid): Contrary
to popular belief, stress will result in loss of stomach acid production.
Achlorhydria is also a natural process of aging and perhaps the most
significant aging phenomenon. Seventy-five percent of people over the age
of 50 years require supplementation of stomach acid.

claims.claim_text: Chronic dyspepsia — what it costs if you leave it. Dyspepsia means poor digestion, and Wallach describes it by its everyday signs: belching, burping, bloating and 'acid stomach.' His explanation inverts the usual one — the trouble is not too much acid but that the stomach's acid is not acid enough, so food ferments and the gas is burped back up. He calls it probably the most common 'disease' in the western world and certainly the most costly, measured by what people spend on relief — but says the real cost is what it becomes: food allergies, osteoporosis, anemia, a debilitated immune system, degenerative disease. Prevention is reduced stress, exercise, healthful diet habits and reasonable food volumes; and because stomach-acid production falls as we age — an unforgiving event, and the main cause of dyspepsia in seniors — the regular use of digestive aids.
claims.verbatim:
Dyspepsia is probably the most common
“disease” in the western world and is certainly the most costly from the
amount of money spent on “relief.” Even more costly is the secondary
results of chronic dyspepsia: food allergies, osteoporosis, anemia,
debilitated immune system, degenerative disease. Prevention includes
reduced stress levels, exercise, healthful diet habits, and reasonable food
volumes. An unforgiving event as we age is a decrease in stomach acid
production, the main cause of dyspepsia in seniors. Prevention in this case
includes the regular use of digestive aids.

claims.claim_text: Antacids versus digestive aids. Wallach's position on antacids is split, and the split follows from his account of indigestion. In an emergency they are a good temporary fix. As a regular habit they harm you — regular use will eventually damage you by reducing the nutrients you absorb — because the stomach's acid is already not acid enough, so neutralizing it further undercuts the digestion and absorption that acid exists to drive. What he prescribes instead is replacement rather than suppression: 75 to 200 mg of betaine hydrochloride (a supplemental form of stomach acid) with pancreatic enzymes, three times a day, 15 to 30 minutes before each meal. His herbal preventions and remedies are papaya, common barberry, and bitters such as gentian — and in some cases a glass of wine or several ounces of vinegar before meals will help.
claims.verbatim:
Treatment of dyspepsia includes supplementation of 75-200 mg betaine
HCl and pancreatic enzymes t.i.d. 15-30 minutes before each meal.
“Antacids” are a good “temporary fix” in an emergency, but regular use will
eventually damage you by reducing the nutrients you absorb.

claims.claim_text: Who should take digestive aids, and why. Wallach gives this instruction as part of preventing candidiasis — the Candida albicans overgrowth he ties to chronic fatigue syndrome — and the reasoning is what makes the advice land. Candida is a normally harmless yeast living on the skin, mouth, vagina and intestine. It turns pathological when the gut's competing normal bacteria are killed off by long-term antibiotic use, or when low stomach acid (hypochlorhydria, usually the result of salt restriction) lets it move up into the stomach — a location it does not normally occupy. Stress reduces stomach acid once it reaches the point of decompensation, and food allergies change the lining of the gut in a way very similar to celiac disease, raising the nutrient concentration in the gut into a 'hyperfertilized' environment the yeast finds attractive; eventually the overgrowth spills into the bloodstream. So his prevention starts with knowing your own digestive and absorptive patterns: pulse-test for food allergies, avoid long-term antibiotics, and as you grow older take betaine HCl and pancreatic enzymes before meals to offset the normal decrease in stomach-acid production. He is emphatic on two more points — take these digestive aids if you are under stress, and deal aggressively with any disease that lowers your immune capacity.
claims.verbatim:
Prevention includes being aware of your intestines and knowing your
digestive and absorptive abilities and patterns. Do pulse tests for food
allergies, avoid long term use of antibiotics, and as you grow older take
betaine HCl and pancreatic enzymes before meals to offset the normal
decrease in production of stomach acid. Be sure to take these digestive aids
if you are under stress; deal aggressively with any disease that lowers your
immune capacity!

claims.claim_text: Gastric bloating — where the gas actually comes from. Bloating is the accumulation of gas in the stomach, and Wallach's explanation turns on a fact most people don't know: a healthy stomach is sterile, and it stays that way because it is so acidic. When hypochlorhydria — low stomach acid — sets in, that sterility fails, and bacteria and yeast from the small intestine migrate upward into the stomach, a place they do not belong. There they ferment the carbohydrates and sugars you have eaten, and the gas that fermentation produces is the 'bloat.' It is the same picture he draws for achlorhydria, where the symptom triad is 'burp, belch, and bloat,' and it explains why his treatment goes after the missing acid — colloidal minerals, betaine HCl and pancreatic enzymes before meals — rather than after the gas.
claims.verbatim:
BLOATING (gastric) is the accumulation of gas in the stomach. Normally
the stomach is sterile because of the acid environment; however, when
hypochlorhydria (low stomach acid) occurs, bacteria and yeast from the
small intestine migrates up into the stomach. The bacteria in the stomach
now “ferments” carbohydrates and sugars that are eaten and produce gas or
“bloat.”

claims.claim_text: Dumping syndrome — why an acid intestine disables your enzymes. Dumping syndrome is the sudden emptying of stomach contents into the small intestine all at once, overloading the intestine's natural buffer system. That matters because of where the body's acid is meant to sit: the stomach is supposed to be strongly acidic, the small intestine is not, and pancreatic enzymes require an alkaline environment to function — so when unbuffered acid floods in, they stop working properly. Wallach notes it is a common side effect of stomach surgery, and that anemia and osteoporosis are its common secondary diseases, which is what you would expect from a stretch of gut that can no longer digest and absorb. His treatment works with the mechanism rather than against it: any of the classic bitters such as gentian, folic acid at 3 to 5 mg a day, pectin at half an ounce in water before meals, high animal-protein diets, six to eight small meals a day rather than a few large ones, and lying down for half an hour after eating.
claims.verbatim:
DUMPING SYNDROME is the sudden “dumping” of stomach contents
into the small intestine all at once, thus overloading the natural intestinal
buffer system. The resulting acid condition in the intestine prevents proper
functioning of pancreatic enzymes, which require an alkaline environment.
Dumping syndrome is a common side effect of stomach surgery. Anemia
and osteoporosis are common secondary diseases of the dumping
syndrome.

claims.claim_text: How acidic your stomach is supposed to be. Wallach draws a sharp line between the body's internal chemistry and its secretions. Internally, acidity is policed within a very narrow range: healthy blood runs 7.36 to 7.44, below 7.30 is acidosis, above 7.44 is alkalosis, and anything below 6.8 or above 7.8 is rapidly fatal. Secretions and excretions are the opposite — deliberately variable, running from about 1.0 in stomach acid at one end to 8.2 in pancreatic juice at the other, with alkaline urine in vegans. That spread is the point rather than a flaw. The stomach is meant to be strongly acidic: it is the acid environment that keeps the stomach sterile and that activates protein digestion. The pancreatic juice meeting food further down the tract is meant to be alkaline — which is why acid conditions in the small intestine disable pancreatic enzymes.
claims.verbatim:
In contrast to the internal body, the pH
of secretions and excretions can be more variable and range from 1.0 in
stomach acid to 8.2 in pancreatic juice and alkaline urine in vegans.
